scenes.title: Key ideas
items: Name services (e.g. an ENS name) are convenient but make an address easy to find and…
scenes.vo: First, Blockchains are public. Anyone who links an address to you can see its balance and history, forever. Next, Link less: don't post addresses, screenshots or wins publicly; use separate addresses for public activity (for example donations, NFTs) and for savings; be aware that exchange withdrawals link your identity (K.Y.C.) to the receiving address. Then, Name services (for example an ENS name) are convenient but make an address easy to find and associate with you. Also, Physical risk ("wrench attacks"): criminals target people known to hold crypto. Low profile is the first defence. Multisig with keys in separate locations means no single person can be forced to move everything. And finally, Home and devices: hardware wallets and backups out of sight; encrypted devices; don't discuss holdings with people who don't need to know.

scenes.vo: Let's work an example, step by step. Alex posts a screenshot of a big win, with the address visible. Anyone can now see Alex's balance and follow every future move, and scammers and thieves now have a target. Better: no screenshots, a vault address that has never been shared, and a 2-of-3 multisig so no single key holder can be coerced into draining it.

scenes.title: Checklist
items: Savings addresses have never been posted or linked publicly
No holdings screenshots or wins on social media
Vault keys held so no single person can move everything
Backups stored discreetly, away from where people would look
